newsitem.title: UK: Flags of division over Portadown.
newsitem.headline: Flags of division over Portadown.

text.p: Rival Irish and British flags flew in troubled Portadown on Saturday as Northern Ireland braced itself for a Sunday that could herald conflict or compromise.
Along Garvaghy Road, a half-mile (one km) highway bounded by sprawling housing estates, Irish tricolours fluttered from every lampost signposting it as a Catholic enclave.
Protestant "Orangemen", whose fathers walked the road when it was open fields, are determined to parade through it on Sunday and the British province is on tenterhooks.
Nationalists see the 200-year-old Orange Order, the province's exclusively Protestant marching brotherhood, as bigoted and supremacist and say they should march in their own areas.
Orangemen say they only want to march to and from a church service and that Catholic protests are engineered by militant republicans bent on destroying their "British heritage".
For a third successive year the Orange Order's disputed parade from Drumcree on the edge of Portadown through Garvaghy Road is fuelling tension and fears of violence engulfing the province.
Last year Britain banned the march for four days, and reaped a whirwind of Protestant street violence.
Police backed down after four days, allowed the march through the Catholic zone, and that in turn ignite a frenzy of Catholic rioting.

Troops in armoured personnel carriers and police in landrovers were drafted into the country lanes around Drumcree church overnight, where Orangemen are due to worship on Sunday, and on approach roads to Garvaghy Road as tension rose.

The "Loyalist" Corcrain estate near Garvaghy Road was awash with British flags, the town centre was criss-crossed in red- white-and-blue streamers and two "Union Jack" British flags billowed from the belfry of Drumcree church.
A Protestant man seated on the sill of his window in a tight-terraced "Loyalist" street, said he hoped the British government would allow the Orangemen to parade through.
"It's a public road, it's the Queen's highway," he said, incredulous at the thought of Orangemen being blocked.
A Catholic woman on the Garvaghy Road said she now felt that the British authorities would order the Protestants marchers to stay out. "I hope to God that they re-route that pararde."
Two months ago a young Catholic man was kicked to death by a mob of "Loyalist" thugs late at night in the town cenre.
Last month Irish Republican Army guerillas, who are backed by some of the province's Catholics, murdered two policemen in the nearby town of Lurgan.
Protestants said that the IRA was deliberately trying to foment problem during the "marching season".
Orangemen stoutly deny Catholic charges that they march simply "to show who is master". They vow that their planned Sunday march would be short, solemn and quiet.,
Most of Portadown's Catholic minority live on the Garvaghy road and they have laid plans for a "street festival" coinciding with the march.
Murals were painted on overnight in preparation for the festival, one of them proclaiming "failte go dti Garbh Achaid" - which is Irish for "welcome to Garvaghy".
But the Orangemen know there is no welcome for them.
